name: app.scrapa/scrapa
title: scrapa.app
description: Read web pages as markdown, search the web, list a site's URLs and run a real Chrome.

tools.name: scrape
tools.description: Read one web page and hand it back as markdown, HTML, plain text, its links, a screenshot, a PDF, or the fields you ask for, read off the page by a model. `engine: "auto"` (the default) makes a plain HTTP request first and re-reads the page in a real Chromium when the body turns out to be a JavaScript shell, so you pay for a browser only when the page needed one. To send a search form or a JSON query, use `method: "POST"` with a `body`; to download a file exactly as the site sent it, ask for `formats: ["raw"]`. A link to a PDF or a Word file is read into text too, headings and paragraphs included. To click a cookie banner, type into a search box or run a script before the page is read, send `browser.actions`. Every request leaves through a residential proxy, or through your own with `proxy: { pool: "custom", server }`. The answer says which engine replied, where the page finally was and what it cost.

url.description: The page to read. An http(s) URL. Private and loopback hosts are refused.

engine.description: How to read it. "fetch" is a plain HTTP request; "browser" renders the page in a real Chromium; "auto" (the default) fetches first and escalates to the browser when the body turns out to be a JavaScript shell, billing whichever engine answered. A POST and "raw" always use "fetch", so leave it out for them.

escalate.description: Whether to try again a different way when the first attempt is blocked. On by default. `false` stops after one try. The site's refusal is your answer, and it costs nothing, unless your own `browser.actions` script ran in the page first. It is how you bound a call: with `auto`, trying again is what charges the browser price instead of the fetch one. A POST is sent once, so it is off for a POST.

method.description: The HTTP method. "POST" sends `body` to the URL, for a search form or a JSON query. It is sent once: never retried and never sent again another way, because sending it twice could repeat what it did.

body.description: What a POST sends, at most 64 KB. Set its type in `headers`: `{"content-type": "application/json"}` for JSON, or `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` for a form. If the site redirects, a 301, 302 or 303 reads the next page with GET and without the body; a 307 or 308 sends it again only if the protocol, host and port stay the same, and otherwise stops and names the new address.

retry.description: How many extra tries to give a page the site blocks, each from a different address. 0 (the default) takes the site's first no as the answer. A blocked page costs nothing, so a try that is blocked again is free, but it takes as long as the first one did, so the call can run that many times longer. Once your `browser.actions` steps click, type, press a key or run a script on a page, it is not tried again, so nothing is done twice. If one of your scripts ran in it, the block is charged.

formats.description: What to hand back. "screenshot" and "pdf" come back as base64 and need the browser engine; asking for both costs no more than one. "extract" is the page read into fields by a model, and needs an `extract` block saying which ones. A link to a PDF or a Word (.docx) file is read into text, so the text formats work on it too. We read files up to 25 MB, and from a PDF the first 200 pages and the first 5 million characters. Reading a file costs what the engine costs: 1 credit with fetch, 5 with the browser. A Word file that holds more than 32 MB once unzipped answers FILE_TOO_LARGE, and a file link that answers a short web page instead of the file answers UPSTREAM_BLOCKED, both at no charge. A dead link is the exception: its 404 or 410 page is the site's answer, and comes back with that status at the fetch price. "raw" is the file exactly as the site sent it, as base64 with its content type: a PDF report, an image, a spreadsheet. It uses the fetch engine and holds up to 5 MB; a larger file answers FILE_TOO_LARGE at no charge, never cut short.

onlyMainContent.description: Read only the page's main content into `markdown`, `text` and `extract`: the article or the product, without the menus, ads and related links around it. On by default. Set `false` for the whole page. When the main content is under 50 words, you get the whole page instead. `html` and `links` always hold the whole page.

includeTags.description: CSS selectors for the parts of the page to keep, such as `["h1", ".price"]`. `markdown`, `text` and `extract` then hold only what they match, in page order, and `onlyMainContent` no longer applies. Hidden parts are never kept. Up to 20 selectors, 256 characters each.

excludeTags.description: CSS selectors for the parts of the page to leave out of `markdown`, `text` and `extract`, such as `[".comments", "#newsletter"]`. Up to 20 selectors, 256 characters each.

expect.description: What the page should answer with. Set `"json"` when you are reading an API: anything else that comes back (a maintenance notice, a "checking your browser" page, a login form) is then not your answer. It costs nothing, and we try again from another address instead of handing you a page you cannot parse. Without it, whatever the page returns is your answer.

extract.description: What to pull out of the page, for the "extract" format. A model reads the page and fills in the shape you asked for. Give it a JSON Schema, a sentence, or both. It reads what the page says; it does not do arithmetic over it, so ask for the numbers and add them up in your own code.

schema.description: The shape you want back, as JSON Schema: an object whose properties are the fields you need. A field the page does not mention comes back null; nothing is invented to fill it.

prompt.description: What to pull out, in your own words: `the price, the author and the date it was published`. Use it on its own for a quick read, or beside `schema` to say what a field means.

proxy.description: Where the request leaves from. Defaults to the managed residential pool.

pool.description: Which exit to leave through. "residential" is the managed pool, metered by the megabyte; "custom" is your own proxy, free on every plan, bytes never billed.

server.description: Your own proxy, `http(s)://[user:pass@]host:port`. Required for pool "custom", refused for the managed one.

country.description: Where the call should look like it comes from, ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 (`us`, `br`). Name one and the managed pool leaves from that country. Leave it out and the page sees a US browser, from an address we pick. A scrape or a map on the managed pool makes one exception: a site whose address ends in `.br`, `.de`, `.es`, `.fr`, `.it`, `.jp`, `.nl`, `.pl` or `.uk` is read from its own country. The browser's clock and languages follow the country on every pool.

state.description: A state or region inside `country`, by name: `california`, `são paulo`. Managed pool only. Spell the name out, since an abbreviation like `sp` finds nobody. In the US and Brazil the browser's clock follows the state.

city.description: A city inside `country`, by name: `curitiba`, `new york`. Managed pool only. Most calls leave from that city and a few from elsewhere in its state, as the pool's own location data places them. A place with nobody in it right now answers `PROXY_REFUSED` at no charge; ask for the state or the country alone.

browser.description: How to render it. Only the browser engine reads these. With `auto` they apply if the page turns out to need one, except `actions`, which always use the browser.

waitUntil.description: When the page counts as loaded. "load" (the default) waits for images and stylesheets; "domcontentloaded" is the fastest and stops at the HTML; "networkidle" waits until the page stops asking for things. Every page gets a short settle after this whichever you pick.

waitForSelector.description: Wait until this CSS selector is on the page. It is the dependable way to read something a script draws. If it never shows up, the call comes back as a timeout at no charge, rather than the half-built page.

waitMs.description: Wait this many milliseconds after the page settles, for the scripts no selector describes. It comes out of `timeoutMs`, never on top of it.

viewport.description: The window size the page is rendered in, 1280×800 unless you say. Set it when a site serves a different layout by width.

fullPage.description: Screenshot the whole scrollable page instead of just the window. A long page makes a large answer: the image comes back as base64 inside the response.

milliseconds.description: How long to wait, in milliseconds. All the waits together have to fit inside `timeoutMs`.

selector.description: Wait until this CSS selector is on the page. If it never shows up, the step fails.

oneOf.description: Wait a fixed time, or until a CSS selector is on the page. Give `milliseconds` or `selector`, not both.

selector.description: The CSS selector of what to click. The first match gets the click, and the step waits for it to show up.

all.description: Click every visible match, not just the first. A selector that matches nothing is then not an error, which suits a cookie banner only some visitors see.

oneOf.description: Click something on the page.

text.description: What to type, up to 1,000 characters.

oneOf.description: Type text into the field that has focus. Click the field in the step before this one.

key.description: The key's name: "Enter", "Tab", "Escape", "ArrowDown", or two together such as "Control+A".

oneOf.description: Press a key.

selector.description: Scroll this element instead of the whole page, such as a list with its own scroll bar.

oneOf.description: Scroll one screen up or down.

fullPage.description: Take the whole scrollable page instead of just the window.

oneOf.description: Take a screenshot at this point. It comes back in `actions.screenshots`, as base64.
Keep the page's address and HTML at this point. They come back in `actions.scrapes`. All the scrape steps in one call can keep 5 MB of HTML together.

script.description: The body of an async function, up to 8,000 characters, such as `return document.title`. It runs in the page, beside the page's own scripts. What it returns comes back in `actions.javascriptReturns` as JSON, or as null when JSON cannot hold it. All the scripts in one call can return 64 KB together. Once a script starts, the call is charged even if that script throws, a later step fails, the page crashes or times out, the site blocks it, the script leads to an address we refuse, your own proxy says no, or an `includeTags` or `excludeTags` selector is too slow for the page it built, because the script may already have read the page. A failure on our side (a 5xx) is still refunded.

oneOf.description: Run your own JavaScript in the page.

actions.description: Steps to run in the page before it is read, in the order you list them. A step can wait, click, type, press a key, scroll, take a screenshot, keep the HTML or run a script. Steps always use the browser engine, at the browser price. The formats you ask for read the page as the last step left it. Up to 50 steps, at most 10 of them screenshots or scrapes. If one fails, the call answers ACTION_FAILED, which names the step and why. That costs nothing, unless one of your scripts started, the one that failed included: then the call is charged.

headers.description: Extra request headers to send to the page, such as an authorization token, a cookie or a custom user agent. The connection's own headers cannot be set.

timeoutMs.description: How long to give the page before giving up, in milliseconds. A page that never arrives costs nothing, unless your own `browser.actions` script ran in the page first.

maxAge.description: The oldest copy of the page you accept, in milliseconds, up to 3600000 (one hour). If we still hold a copy of the same URL that your account read within that time, from the same country and with the same engine, you get it back for 0 credits and the answer says `cached: true`. If not, we read the page now and keep a copy for up to an hour, unless the page still needs JavaScript (`metadata.needsJs`). We may drop a copy sooner, to make room or on a deploy, and a batch keeps its own copies, apart from single calls. `0` always reads the page now, and keeps the copy for the calls after it. `extract` is still charged, because the model reads the copy again. Leave `maxAge` out to read the page fresh every time. A POST, or a call with `headers`, your own proxy, `browser` options, a screenshot, a PDF, `raw` or `escalate: false`, is always read fresh.

tools.name: quote_scrape
tools.description: What the same request would cost, without making it. Free, and refused by the same guards a real call meets, so a quote is never a price for a call that would be denied. `maxCost` is the ceiling: for `auto` it is the browser's price, which is only charged if the page turns out to need one. With `maxAge`, the quote is the price of reading the page now; if a copy is there, the page costs nothing and only `extract` is charged.

tools.name: map_site
tools.description: Hand back every URL a site lists, without reading the pages: what its robots.txt and sitemaps name (gzipped ones too, and indexes of sitemaps), plus the links on the page you named. Each URL comes back once, without tracking parameters or a trailing slash, with `lastmod` when the sitemap gives one. Only the host you named is kept unless you set `includeSubdomains`, and `search` keeps the URLs that contain a word. To read a page, pass its URL to `scrape`.

url.description: The site to map, as any http(s) URL on it. Private and loopback hosts are refused.

limit.description: How many URLs to hand back at most, 1 to 30,000. The price is the same whatever you ask for.

search.description: Only URLs that contain this text, upper or lower case alike: `blog` keeps `/blog/` and `/Blog-post`.

includeSubdomains.description: Also keep URLs on other hosts of the same domain, like `blog.example.com` for `example.com`. Off by default: only the host you named, with or without `www.`.

sitemap.description: Where to look. "include" reads the site's sitemaps and the links on the page you named; "only" reads the sitemaps alone; "skip" reads the page's links alone.

proxy.description: Where the map's requests leave from. Every file it reads goes through the same exit.

pool.description: Which exit to leave through. "residential" is the managed pool, metered by the megabyte; "custom" is your own proxy, free on every plan, bytes never billed.

server.description: Your own proxy, `http(s)://[user:pass@]host:port`. Required for pool "custom", refused for the managed one.

country.description: Where the call should look like it comes from, ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 (`us`, `br`). Name one and the managed pool leaves from that country. Leave it out and the page sees a US browser, from an address we pick. A scrape or a map on the managed pool makes one exception: a site whose address ends in `.br`, `.de`, `.es`, `.fr`, `.it`, `.jp`, `.nl`, `.pl` or `.uk` is read from its own country. The browser's clock and languages follow the country on every pool.

tools.name: search
tools.description: Ask the web a question and get back ranked results: title, URL and the snippet the index holds. They are read live off a real search front through a residential exit, never a reseller's cache. `country` picks both the exit and the market, so `br` returns what somebody in Brazil would see. Narrow to your own list of hosts with `includeDomains`, ask for `topic: "news"` when you want dated journalism or `topic: "images"` when you want pictures, and add `answer: true` when you want a paragraph written over the results instead of writing it yourself. To read a result, pass its URL to `scrape`.

query.description: What to search for, in plain words: the same thing you would type.

limit.description: How many results to hand back at most, 1–20. Billed per 10, so asking for more than 10 costs a second row. Fewer can come back than you asked for: an index has what it has, and `includeDomains` filters what it returns.

topic.description: What kind of results. "general" is the web; "news" is dated journalism, and the only topic that reliably carries `publishedAt`; "images" is pictures: each result is the page that shows one, with the picture's own address, a thumbnail and its size in `image`. Pictures the engine marks as adult are left out.

timeRange.description: Only pages from the last day, week, month or year. Absent is any time.

includeDomains.description: Only results on these hosts, bare (`linkedin.com`). Subdomains are included. Asked of the search front AND enforced on the answer, so what comes back is on your list whatever the front did with it. With `topic: "images"` it takes one host.

answer.description: Also write a short paragraph answering the query from the results, in the query's language. Costs one extra credit; leave it off when your own model reads the snippets.

proxy.description: Where the search leaves from. `country` picks the exit AND the market the front answers for. `br` gets Brazilian results in Portuguese.

pool.description: Which exit to leave through. "residential" is the managed pool, metered by the megabyte; "custom" is your own proxy, free on every plan, bytes never billed.

server.description: Your own proxy, `http(s)://[user:pass@]host:port`. Required for pool "custom", refused for the managed one.

tools.name: create_batch

The site's refusal is your answer, and it costs nothing, unless your own `browser.actions` script ran in the page first. It is how you bound a call: with `auto`, trying again is what charges the browser price instead of the fetch one. A POST is sent once, so it is off for a POST.

retry.description: How many extra tries to give a page the site blocks, each from a different address. 0 (the default) takes the site's first no as the answer. A blocked page costs nothing, so a try that is blocked again is free, but it takes as long as the first one did, so the call can run that many times longer. Once your `browser.actions` steps click, type, press a key or run a script on a page, it is not tried again, so nothing is done twice. If one of your scripts ran in it, the block is charged.

formats.description: What to hand back. "screenshot" and "pdf" come back as base64 and need the browser engine; asking for both costs no more than one. We read files up to 25 MB, and from a PDF the first 200 pages and the first 5 million characters. Reading a file costs what the engine costs: 1 credit with fetch, 5 with the browser. extract.description: What to pull out of the page, for the "extract" format. A model reads the page and fills in the shape you asked for. Give it a JSON Schema, a sentence, or both. server.description: Your own proxy, `http(s)://[user:pass@]host:port`. Required for pool "custom", refused for the managed one.
